Figure 1-4 shows the evolution of the U.S. federal budget surplus (a negative value represents a deficit) since 1990. You can see that after an increase in deficits due to the 1990–1991 recession, the rest of the decade was associated with a steady improvement and by 1998, the budget had actually gone from deficit to surplus. Figure 2-1 plots the evolution of both nominal GDP and real GDP since 1960. By construction, the two are equal in 2005. The figure shows that real GDP in 2010 was about 4.7 times its level of 1960—a considerable increase, but clearly much less than the 28-fold increase in nominal GDP over the same period. Figure 2-3 shows the evolution of unemployment in the United States since 1970. Since 1960, the U.S. unemployment rate has fluctuated between 3 and 10%, going up during recessions and down during expansions. Again, you can see the effect of the crisis, with the unemployment rate reaching a peak at nearly 10% in 2010, the highest such rate since the 1980s. Why Do Economists Care about Unemployment?

Table A-3 extends the budget figures discussed in Document 1. The deficit peaked in 2009 and then narrowed every year, as revenues recovered with output and crisis-related spending was phased out. By 2013 the deficit was back below 5% of GDP, the level Document 1 expected to be reached only "by the middle of the decade". Table B-2 reports our calculations of the U.S. unemployment and participation rates as annual averages from household survey data. Participation fell by 1.3 percentage points between 2007 and 2010. Some workers who lost their jobs stopped looking for work and therefore are not counted as unemployed.
